one_liner: Kepler-era CUDA device-side slab allocator (hamalloc/hafree) for small blocks, built to beat in-kernel CUDA malloc on throughput.
what_it_does: A malloc/free-style allocator that kernels call: hamalloc(size_t) and hafree(void*) are __device__ functions, and allocations persist across kernel launches. The host calls ha_init(halloc_opts_t) once to reserve memory, by default 512 MiB capped at 3/4 of device memory, with 75% for halloc slabs and 25% left to the CUDA heap. Requests up to 3072 bytes are served from halloc's slabs; larger ones are forwarded to CUDA's device malloc. It ships as a static library (libhalloc.a) and needs relocatable device code (-rdc / -dc).
how_it_is_fast: Memory is split into 4 MiB slabs (superblocks), each serving one size class. Size classes are 2x or 3x a power-of-two unit, from 16 to 3072 bytes. Free chunks are tracked in per-slab bit arrays. A thread picks a starting chunk by hashing a warp-aggregated per-size counter, claims it with one atomicOr, and on collision re-probes with a size-specific hash step, so threads spread over the slab instead of contending on a list head. Slabs move between free, sparse, roomy and busy sets by occupancy thresholds (0.012, 0.6, 0.835). The leader lane of a warp swaps in a new head slab for every lane of the same size, and hafree is a single atomicAnd on the bit array plus a counter decrement.
when_to_use: Kernels that make many small (16-256 B) device-side allocations from tens of thousands of threads, such as dynamic graphs, per-thread lists or particle buffers, on Kepler/Pascal-class GPUs.
Replacing in-kernel CUDA malloc when allocation throughput is the bottleneck and the heap stays well below its reserved capacity.
Research baselines: it is one of the standard allocators in GPU allocator surveys (Winter et al. PPoPP 2021, memmansurvey).
when_not_to_use: Volta and newer GPUs with stock code: it uses the pre-CUDA-9 warp intrinsics (__ballot, __any, __shfl, PTX without .sync) and warp-synchronous loops. Issue #3 reports hangs on a TITAN V (CUDA 10.2) for sizes above 256 B at 10K threads and above 32 B at 100K threads, and the memmansurvey port notes the masks 'are quite hard to translate to modern CUDA' and it only works in its sync build.

Modern CUDA toolkits without makefile edits: it builds for sm_20/sm_30/sm_35 only (sm_20 was dropped in CUDA 9 and sm_30 in CUDA 11), and issue #1 reports the build failing on an empty bin/ directory.
Heaps that run near full: search snippets of later papers say halloc fails to allocate beyond about 50% utilization (not verified here, papers blocked).
Allocations above 3 KiB: they go to CUDA's own allocator and get no speedup.
Workloads that need to resize the heap or release memory: there is no way to grow after ha_init, and ha_shutdown is a no-op.

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (device runtime malloc for large blocks); tests use thrust
integration.min_toolchain: CUDA 5.0+ (tested 6.5), nvcc with -rdc=true; README requires compute capability 2.0+
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs; tested on CC 3.5 (K20X, K40); user report of tests passing on GTX 1070 (sm_61, CUDA 10.1) after makefile edits; hangs reported on Volta (sm_70)
integration.thread_safety: hamalloc/hafree are thread-safe across threads and concurrent kernels per README; relies on pre-Volta lockstep warp execution
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same semantics as device malloc/free but different names (hamalloc/hafree), needs ha_init first, and pointers cannot be freed with free/cudaFree; the malloc/free and operator new overrides in halloc.h are disabled as unstable

gotchas: ha_init calls cudaDeviceSetCacheConfig(cudaFuncCachePreferL1) for the whole device and sets cudaLimitMallocHeapSize to the 25% remainder, which silently changes the behaviour of the rest of your program.
Licence correction: LICENSE.txt offers a choice of GPL-2.0 or the OpenIB.org BSD licence (Forschungszentrum Juelich, 2015), so the code can be used under BSD terms, not only GPL-2.0.

Host-side init bug in halloc.cu: `memset(sbs, 0xff, MAX_NSBS * sizeof(uint))` targets sbs instead of the just-malloc'd sb_counters, so counters for unreserved slab slots are left uninitialized. It looks harmless for slabs actually reserved, and it does not touch the measured fast path.

Size classes are 2u/3u steps, so internal waste is up to about a third (for example 49 B rounds to 64 B); the library was tuned with -Xptxas -maxrregcount=64 and -dlcm=cg, and the register count matters for occupancy of the calling kernel.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only GPU device-side general allocator among the catalogued siblings. LLFree targets the Linux kernel page allocator and the others are CPU mallocs, so pick halloc only for in-kernel CUDA allocation on pre-Volta hardware (or after porting to *_sync intrinsics).
verified_claims_summary: First-party only: the README claims more than 1.5 billion mallocs/s and more than 1 billion malloc/free pairs/s for 16-byte allocations by tens of thousands of threads with more than 100 MiB allocated on a K20X, and calls this 'much higher' than other GPU allocators without giving CUDA-malloc or competitor numbers. Perf drivers (throughput, phase-throughput and others) are in tst/perf. Independent comparisons exist in the Gelado-Garland 2019 and Winter et al. 2021 papers, but those were blocked here; snippets only.
status_note: Abandoned since 2015-01-28 and dual GPL-2.0/BSD-licensed, so copyable; usable on Kepler/Pascal, needs a warp-intrinsic port for Volta+ and a makefile update for current CUDA.
